brief.topic: A Balance Has Three Ways to Answer

s01: One of these nine coins is heavier.
There is a lovely way to find it in two weighings.
Instead of splitting into two piles,
Make three groups of three instead.
Weigh the first group against the second.
the heavy coin must be in the untouched group.
Every answer leaves exactly three suspects.
Let us take the balanced branch.
the untouched ninth coin is the heavier one.
The trick is using balance as information,
not treating it as a failed experiment.
This assumes exactly one coin is heavier,
and all the others weigh the same.
If the odd coin might be lighter,
this strategy no longer solves the same problem.
What about twenty seven coins with one known heavier?
Three equal groups reduce them to nine.

scenes.narration: One of these nine coins is heavier. There is a lovely way to find it in two weighings. Instead of splitting into two piles, notice something about a balance: it has three possible answers. Left heavy, right heavy, or balanced. Make three groups of three instead. Weigh the first group against the second. If the left side drops, keep those three coins. If the right side drops, keep those three. If they balance, the heavy coin must be in the untouched group. Every answer leaves exactly three suspects. Let us take the balanced branch. Coins seven, eight, and nine are still possible. Now weigh seven against eight. If seven drops, it is the heavy coin. If eight drops, it is eight. And if they balance, the untouched ninth coin is the heavier one. Here, eight drops. Two weighings, one answer. The trick is using balance as information, not treating it as a failed experiment. Three outcomes, followed by three outcomes, can distinguish nine possibilities. This assumes exactly one coin is heavier, and all the others weigh the same. If the odd coin might be lighter, this strategy no longer solves the same problem. What about twenty seven coins with one known heavier? Three equal groups reduce them to nine. So three weighings are enough.
